title: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst and Congenital Neck Masses
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the thyroid descends from the tongue to the lower neck and how a remnant of that path becomes a thyroglossal duct cyst. It then separates this midline cyst from the lateral branchial cleft cyst and from ectopic thyroid tissue, which can sit on the same midline path and may be the patient's only thyroid. Board questions describe a neck lump by its position and by what makes it move, then ask for the embryologic origin, the likely complication, or the finding that must be checked first. If you can trace the route of thyroid descent and the fate of the second pharyngeal cleft, you can answer most of them.
prerequisites: Pharyngeal arches, clefts, and pouches and their derivatives
Surface anatomy of the tongue, hyoid bone, larynx, and sternocleidomastoid
Thyroid follicle histology (EN-2) and iodide uptake by follicular cells (EN-8)
Hypothalamic, pituitary, and thyroid feedback (TRH, TSH, T4, T3)

connections.how: Follicular cells concentrate iodide through the sodium iodide symporter, which is why a radionuclide scan can locate any functioning thyroid tissue, wherever it lies.
Thyroid dysgenesis, including ectopic thyroid, is a leading cause of congenital hypothyroidism, and removing the only thyroid tissue causes permanent primary hypothyroidism.
Follicular cells left in the cyst wall are the source of the rare papillary carcinoma that arises in a thyroglossal duct cyst.
The same overgrowth of the second pharyngeal arch that shapes the lateral neck explains the position and tract of branchial cleft cysts and fistulas.

terms.def: A small blind pit at the apex of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis of the tongue that marks the site where the thyroid began.
The endodermal outgrowth from the floor of the primitive pharynx that descends to form the thyroid gland.
The narrow epithelial tube that connects the descending thyroid to the tongue and normally becomes solid and disappears.
A fluid-filled cyst formed by a persistent segment of the thyroglossal duct, located in or near the midline.
A normal upward extension of thyroid tissue from the isthmus that represents the lower end of the thyroglossal duct.
Thyroid tissue left at an abnormal site along the path of descent because descent failed or was incomplete.
Ectopic thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue near the foramen cecum, the most common ectopic site.
A temporary lateral pocket formed when the second pharyngeal arch grows down over the second, third, and fourth clefts.
A lateral neck cyst, usually from a persistent second cleft or cervical sinus, lying along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid.
An abnormal epithelial-lined tract that connects two surfaces, such as the skin and the pharynx or mouth.

sections.title: How a persistent thyroglossal duct forms a midline cyst that moves with the tongue

blocks.text: At about day 24 the thyroid appears as an endodermal thickening in the midline floor of the primitive pharynx, at the point later marked by the foramen cecum of the tongue. It forms a bilobed diverticulum that descends in front of the pharyngeal gut, anterior to the developing hyoid bone and laryngeal cartilages, and reaches the front of the trachea by about week 7.

During descent the gland stays attached to the tongue by the thyroglossal duct, which normally becomes solid and disappears, leaving the foramen cecum above and, in many people, a pyramidal lobe rising from the isthmus below. Because the hyoid forms from the second and third arch cartilages while the duct still exists, the tract usually passes in front of or through the middle of the hyoid body and may loop briefly behind it.

blocks.title: Thyroid descent and the origin of a duct cyst
steps: Endodermal thickening at the future foramen cecum
Bilobed diverticulum descends in front of the pharyngeal gut
Path passes anterior to or through the hyoid body
Gland reaches the front of the trachea by about week 7
Duct normally becomes solid and disappears
A persistent segment keeps secreting and distends into a cyst
blocks.caption: A cyst can form anywhere on this midline path, most often at or just below the hyoid.

blocks.text: If a segment of the duct fails to obliterate, its lining keeps secreting fluid and the segment distends into a cyst. Cysts near the tongue base tend to have stratified squamous lining and lower cysts pseudostratified ciliated columnar (respiratory) lining, both reflecting the endodermal duct. The wall often contains lymphoid tissue and may contain thyroid follicles.

The thyroglossal duct cyst is the most common congenital neck mass in children. It usually appears in childhood, sometimes in adults, as a painless, smooth, midline mass at or just below the hyoid. It rises with swallowing because the suprahyoid muscles lift the hyoid to which it is tethered, and with tongue protrusion because the remnant tract is anchored at the foramen cecum. A thyroid nodule also rises with swallowing, since the pretracheal fascia binds the thyroid to the larynx, but not with tongue protrusion, so tongue protrusion is the more specific sign.

rows: The thyroid descends in the midline

blocks.caption: Each classic finding traces back to the route and attachments of the duct.

blocks.text: Infection is the most common complication. When the upper tract stays open at the foramen cecum, oral bacteria reach the cyst, often after an upper respiratory infection, and the cyst becomes painful and tender and may form an abscess. Rupture or drainage through the skin leaves a thyroglossal sinus on the front of the neck, so such a tract is usually acquired. Rarely, in about 1% of cysts, carcinoma arises in the wall, most often papillary carcinoma from its follicular cells.

blocks.title: From persistent tract to infection and sinus
steps: Upper tract open at the foramen cecum
Oral bacteria enter, often after a respiratory infection
Rupture or drainage through the skin
Persistent sinus on the anterior neck
blocks.caption: Most draining sinuses follow an infected cyst.

blocks.predict: A midline neck lump rises when the patient swallows but stays still when the tongue is protruded. Is this most likely a thyroglossal duct cyst?
blocks.explain: No. Swallowing raises anything bound to the larynx, including the thyroid, but only a mass tethered at the foramen cecum rises with tongue protrusion, so this suggests a thyroid nodule.

sections.title: Midline versus lateral neck cysts and the need to locate the thyroid

blocks.text: Origin of the branchial cleft cyst

Pharyngeal clefts are the ectodermal grooves between the arches. In week 5 the second arch grows down over the second, third, and fourth clefts and fuses with the lower neck, enclosing a temporary pocket, the cervical sinus, which normally disappears. Most branchial anomalies come from a persistent second cleft or cervical sinus, which lies lateral to the midline structures, so the cyst sits along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, usually just below the angle of the mandible.

The cyst (also called a lymphoepithelial cyst) has a squamous or pseudostratified columnar lining and a wall of dense lymphoid tissue with germinal centers, which swells with upper respiratory infections and explains why the cyst enlarges or becomes infected after a cold. It usually presents in older children and young adults and, lacking attachment to the hyoid or tongue, does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion. A complete second cleft fistula runs from the lower anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, between the internal and external carotid arteries, to the tonsillar fossa.

blocks.title: Thyroglossal duct cyst versus second branchial cleft cyst

Midline, at or just below the hyoid

Lymphoid tissue, may contain thyroid follicles
Possibly, if the mass is ectopic thyroid
blocks.caption: Position and movement separate the two at the bedside.

blocks.text: Position has limits: in an adult, a new cystic lateral lump may be a cystic nodal metastasis, for example from oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma or papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Why the normal thyroid must be confirmed first

When descent fails, thyroid tissue remains on the midline path, most often at the tongue base (lingual thyroid) but also near the hyoid, where it can mimic a duct cyst or lie in its wall. Ectopic tissue is often small and marginal in output, and in many patients it is the only functioning thyroid. Ectopy is the most common form of thyroid dysgenesis, a leading cause of congenital hypothyroidism detected by newborn screening.

Removing the only thyroid tissue ends T4 and T3 production. TRH and TSH rise as negative feedback is lost, but no follicular cells remain to respond, so permanent primary hypothyroidism follows. Ultrasound shows whether a bilobed gland lies in front of the trachea, and a scan with iodine-123 or technetium-99m pertechnetate maps all functioning tissue, because follicular cells take up both through the sodium iodide symporter.

blocks.title: Why removing an ectopic gland causes permanent hypothyroidism
steps: Midline mass holds the only functioning thyroid
Lost feedback raises TRH and TSH
No follicular cells remain to respond
Permanent primary hypothyroidism: high TSH, low free T4
blocks.caption: Locating functioning thyroid first breaks this chain.

blocks.title: Worked example: the mass that is the thyroid
blocks.text: A 6-year-old has a painless midline mass just below the hyoid that rises with tongue protrusion. Step 1: midline position and movement with the tongue point to the thyroglossal tract. Step 2: ultrasound shows no thyroid in front of the trachea. Step 3: a pertechnetate scan shows uptake only in the mass, so it is functioning ectopic thyroid. Step 4: TSH is mildly high with low normal free T4, so the gland already struggles to meet demand. Removing it would cause permanent primary hypothyroidism.

blocks.predict: Why does a radionuclide scan, not the examination, show whether a midline mass is the only thyroid?
blocks.explain: Examination shows position and movement, which a cyst and ectopic thyroid share. Only functioning follicular cells concentrate iodide or pertechnetate through the sodium iodide symporter, so uptake maps working thyroid wherever it lies.
blocks.check: The paragraph on removing the only thyroid tissue.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain the presentation. The thyroid is endodermal and descends in the midline from the foramen cecum past the hyoid, so its remnants are midline, tied to the hyoid, and lined by endodermal epithelium. Branchial cleft cysts come from the ectodermal cervical sinus on the side of the neck, so they are lateral, unattached to the hyoid, and rich in lymphoid tissue. Both tend to swell or become infected after upper respiratory infections, the duct cyst because oral bacteria enter a tract open at the foramen cecum and the branchial cyst because its lymphoid wall reacts.

Physiology and pathology decide what is at stake. Ectopic thyroid shares the midline path of the duct cyst, so a mass that looks like a simple cyst may be the patient's whole supply of thyroid hormone, and only imaging based on iodide uptake shows this reliably.

summary: The thyroid arises at about day 24 from endoderm at the future foramen cecum and descends in the midline past the hyoid to the front of the trachea by about week 7.
The thyroglossal duct normally disappears; the pyramidal lobe is a normal remnant of its lower end.
A persistent duct segment keeps secreting and forms a midline cyst, most often at or just below the hyoid.
The cyst rises with swallowing because it is tethered to the hyoid and with tongue protrusion because its tract is anchored at the foramen cecum.
Thyroid nodules rise with swallowing but not with tongue protrusion, so tongue protrusion is the more specific sign.
Infection from oral bacteria is the most common complication and can leave a draining sinus; papillary carcinoma in the cyst is rare.
A second branchial cleft cyst lies laterally along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, has lymphoid tissue in its wall, and does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.
Ectopic thyroid lies on the same midline path and may be the only functioning thyroid, so a normal gland must be confirmed before a midline mass is removed.
Removing the only thyroid tissue causes permanent primary hypothyroidism with high TSH and low free T4.

verify: Timing of thyroid development (appearance at about day 24 and final position by about week 7) follows Langman; other embryology texts give slightly different days.
The fraction of people with a pyramidal lobe is quoted from about 40% to 50% in anatomy texts; the chapter says only that many people have one.
Carcinoma arising in a thyroglossal duct cyst is quoted as about 1% or less; confirm the figure NABNE expects.
Lingual thyroid is described as the only functioning thyroid tissue in roughly 70% of cases in commonly quoted series; the chapter says only that it often is, so confirm any percentage NABNE uses.
Some sources call the thyroglossal duct cyst the most common congenital neck mass overall and others the most common midline congenital neck mass in children; confirm the wording NABNE uses.
Infrahyoid thyroglossal duct cysts may lie slightly off the midline, more often to the left; confirm whether this detail is tested.
The surgical excision that includes the middle of the hyoid body (Sistrunk procedure) is management and belongs to Part II; it is omitted here, so confirm whether Part I questions expect the eponym.
